title: Perfect and pluperfect subjunctive

objectives.can: Recognise perfect and pluperfect subjunctives, active and passive.

explanation.summary: The perfect and pluperfect subjunctive complete the four tenses of the mood. They are built on the perfect stem, as the perfect and pluperfect indicative are, and they stand mostly in subordinate clauses, especially those that look back to something already done. The pluperfect subjunctive in particular is the ordinary form of the Vulgate's *cum audisset*, 'when he had heard'.

sections.heading: Perfect subjunctive active: -erim
body: The perfect subjunctive active is made from the perfect stem plus -erim, -eris, -erit, -erimus, -eritis, -erint. From *baptizavi* (stem *baptizav-*) comes *baptizaverim*; from *feci* comes *fecerim*; from *vidi* comes *viderim*. These are almost the endings of the future perfect indicative, which has -ero, -eris, -erit, -erimus, -eritis, -erint. Only the first person singular is certain by its ending (-erim against -ero); the others are the same in both tenses, and the sentence decides.

That coincidence matters in this library. The analysis of the texts is automatic, and for a form like *fecerit* the analyser has to choose between future perfect indicative and perfect subjunctive. The exercises use only the forms for which the analyser has a single reading, and in the perfect subjunctive these are chiefly forms in -erim, together with a few plurals. Do not take this to mean that the other persons do not occur: they are common, and you will meet them in the readings.

sections.heading: Pluperfect subjunctive active: -issem
body: The pluperfect subjunctive active is the perfect stem plus -issem, -isses, -isset, -issemus, -issetis, -issent. It is easy to recognise: the -iss- in the middle is the sign. From *vidi* comes *vidissem*, and from *misi* comes *misisset*. The endings -em, -es, -et, -emus, -etis, -ent are those of the imperfect subjunctive, which is why the two tenses look alike; the iss makes the difference.

Perfects in -avi, -evi, -ivi often drop the -vi- before -iss-, and the result is shorter: *audivisset* becomes *audisset*, *audivissent* becomes *audissent*. This shortening is regular. It is the usual form in the Vulgate, so *audisset* is the pluperfect subjunctive of *audio*, not a form of some other verb.
The pluperfect subjunctive of *sum* is *fuissem*, *fuisses*, *fuisset* and so on, and the perfect subjunctive is *fuerim*.

sections.heading: The passive: participle and sum
body: The passive of these two tenses is made, like the perfect passive indicative, with the perfect participle and a form of *sum*. For the perfect subjunctive passive the form of *sum* is the present subjunctive: *sim*, *sis*, *sit*, *simus*, *sitis*, *sint*. For the pluperfect subjunctive passive it is the imperfect subjunctive: *essem*, *esses*, *esset*, *essemus*, *essetis*, *essent*. So *ut sint consummati* is a perfect subjunctive passive, 'that they may have been made perfect', and *cum esset desponsata* is a pluperfect subjunctive passive, 'when she had been betrothed'.

In this library the participle and the form of *sum* are two separate words, so these passive forms cannot be drilled as single words. You will find them in the examples and the readings, and in a question or two where the passive forms must be told from the active.

sections.heading: What they are used for
body: The details of the clauses come in later lessons, but a few patterns are already worth knowing. A pluperfect subjunctive after *cum* usually tells what had happened before the main action: *cum audisset Jesus, secessit*, 'when Jesus had heard, he withdrew'. A perfect subjunctive often stands in a clause about something already done, such as an indirect question (*nescio si baptizaverim*, 'I do not know whether I baptized') or a comparison with an imagined past (*quasi viderim*, 'as if I had seen').

Remember that the subjunctive has no single English equivalent. A pluperfect subjunctive may be translated 'had heard', 'would have heard' or 'might have heard', according to the clause. The form says only that the event is earlier and that it stands in a clause where the subjunctive is required.

misunderstandings: A form in -erit is not necessarily a perfect subjunctive. In most persons it could equally be the future perfect indicative, and the clause decides. The first person singular -erim, against -ero, is the only clear marker.
*audisset* is not an error or a different verb. It is the shortened form of *audivisset*, the pluperfect subjunctive of *audio*; the same shortening occurs in other verbs in -ivi or -avi.
The pluperfect subjunctive is not necessarily 'would have'. Many learners translate every one so. After *cum* it is usually just 'had': 'when he had heard'.
The passive forms are two words. A perfect participle alone is not a subjunctive, and *sit* or *esset* alone is not a perfect or pluperfect form. Both words are needed.

deeper.heading: Why the two tenses coincide
body: Grammarians such as Allen and Greenough treat the perfect subjunctive and the future perfect indicative as two tenses that came to share most of their endings in the course of Latin's history. The detail belongs to historical grammar. For reading, what matters is that the endings alone often cannot tell the two apart, and the clause has to.

quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

check.explain: cum with the pluperfect subjunctive usually gives an earlier event: 'when he had heard'. The present or future would need a different tense.

check.prompt: Which feature shows that baptizaverim is subjunctive?

quoted.title: 1 Corinthians
quoted.english: And I baptized also the household of Stephanus; besides, I know not whether I baptized any other.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

check.explain: The future perfect indicative would be baptizavero. -erim is the perfect subjunctive. The conjunction alone does not decide the mood.

check.prompt: Which sign separates misisset from an imperfect subjunctive?

check.explain: The pluperfect subjunctive adds -isset to the perfect stem. The ending -et alone is also found in the imperfect subjunctive (traderet), so it does not decide.

check.explain: sint (present subjunctive of sum) with the perfect participle consummati forms the perfect subjunctive passive. ut introduces the clause but is no part of the verb.

check.explain: audivissent has the perfect stem audiv- and -issent; the -vi- drops out and gives audissent. audirent is the imperfect subjunctive and audiverunt a perfect indicative.

check.prompt: What tense and voice are in cum esset desponsata mater ejus?

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.english: Now the generation of Christ was in this wise. When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child, of the Holy Ghost.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

check.explain: esset (imperfect subjunctive of sum) with the perfect participle desponsata makes the pluperfect passive subjunctive: 'when she had been betrothed'. The perfect passive would use sit.

reading.why: A narrative in which *cum audisset* and similar clauses carry the story, together with the ordinary indicative tenses you already know.
